extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / literate early-18th-century London public interested in manners, education, and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral and social essays (The Spectator) offering judgments about personal behaviour, education, literary genius, and moral allegory, aimed at shaping public taste and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a Woman's Man
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Woman's Man' dresses loose and negligent, has a soft and indolent manner, appears unconcerned, imitates the creature he hopes to betray in conversation, knows family news, performs little officious services, and may carry spirits for sudden indisposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These combined traits (affectation of unconcern, petty officiousness, knowledge of household affairs) mark the successful lover among women; the essay gives examples (Bareface, the 'pleasant Thief') and notes such men often pair wit and inconstancy with those manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical signs of affectation (strutting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific outward marks: an elevated chest, a pinched hat, a measured step, and a sly surveying eye — collectively called 'strutting'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a gentleman displays any one of these, he may be socially dangerous to women; when combined with learning they become particularly seductive and warrant public warning (remove wives/daughters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation for being well with other women as social currency
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's reputation for being 'well with other women' is itself attractive to a woman — being favoured by many increases his desirability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essays explain the psychology: a woman's ambition to win a rival's slave and the fashion of opposition drive imitation and acceptance of a man whose fame shows him favoured elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity and whim as engines of popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some oddity of behaviour, distinctive dress, or impertinent quarrelling for a lady's sake recommends a man to women even when it would make him ridiculous among men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats such singularities as a deliberate social strategy: affectation and visible difference can win female approval though they would harm a man's standing with other men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value distinction: regular visitants vs. 'ruiners' of ladies
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular visitants are unpaid volunteers who provide company; 'ruiners' are accomplished men versed in court/town occurrences, publicly decent but privately dissolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay praises the latter as the choicest spirits of the age (irresistible to women) and distinguishes different social roles men play in female company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women admire trivial excellencies and imitate fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Women often overlook solid virtues and admire trivial, superficial qualities; reading frivolous books and keeping frivolous company fosters an ambition to be 'amiable in imperfection'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This social tendency leads to tolerance of inconstancy and perjury in lovers; it explains why certain types of men succeed despite moral failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good breeding requires consideration of time and place (behaviour at church)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good breeding means adjusting behaviour to time and place; behaviour at church should respect decency and avoid giggling or distracting displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter-writers urge the Spectator to dwell on good breeding and suggest practical enforcement (church-warden holding up his wand) to maintain decorum; anti-pattern: treating church as entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult natural disposition (indoles) when educating youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural disposition to a particular art, science, trade, or profession should be consulted when caring for and educating young people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers and parents should study each child's bent and not force all through the same classical curriculum; failing to discern capacities produces 'Scandal of Letters' — great scholars who lack right understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid corporal punishment; it injures good natures
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporal punishment (the lash) degrades and brutalizes children, extinguishes virtue, and is counterproductive to producing good minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues shame and honour are sufficient and better for maintaining order; examples and scenes of children broken by punishment are used as warnings against the common practice at grammar schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early vocational sorting based on capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should be examined early and, if nature indicates, be sent to a mechanick way of life rather than kept in school and punished until 14–15 regardless of aptitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical policy: dismiss heavy lads sooner, direct them to trades without respect to birth, to avoid debasing innocent children and wasting their potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of latent greatness in youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular youthful behaviours and bold replies (examples: Alexander's reply about kings to run against, Cassius striking a playfellow, Scipio's remark about Marius) indicate a disposition suited to great undertakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay uses historical vignettes to argue that manners and temper in youth can reveal future greatness; educators should attend to such signs rather than punish or misdirect them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a great genius
rubrics_metrics.description: A great genius is one whose natural parts, without assistance of arts or learning, produce works that delight their own time and amaze posterity; such genius is often nobly wild and extravagant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast this with 'bel esprit' (refinement by art/learning) — genuine genius shows original force and may lack the nicety of modern correctness; examples include Homer, certain ancients, and Shakespeare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitfall: do not imitate irregular genius by rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to reproduce the irregularities and extravagant forms of a singular genius (e.g., Pindar) by rule leads to ridiculous and monster-like compositions (the satire of Pindaricks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that moderate writers who strain after the unbounded flights of nature by artificial tricks only produce absurdity; imitation of irregular genius is a category error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bienséance / nicety of decency in modern taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The later rule of 'bienséance' — nicety and exactness in comparisons and allusions — is a modern, colder-climate refinement that moderates force by decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essays acknowledge a trade-off: ancients had force and daring but sometimes indecent similitudes; moderns gain correctness at the cost of some imaginative freedom. This is a criterion for taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegorical moral: life as a bridge with traps
rubrics_metrics.description: Life is presented allegorically as a bridge across Time with many concealed trap-doors near the entrances; many people fall when pursuing bubbles or distracted by passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral teaching: be wary of immediate temptations and traps; those who pursue frivolous pursuits or are driven by passions fall early — instead pursue virtue to reach the 'islands' (mansions) for good men after death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions and vices as persistent obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Envy, avarice, superstition, despair, love, and similar passions are pictured as birds (vultures, harpies, ravens) that hover and infest human life, contributing to people's downfall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these passions as structural hazards on the 'bridge' of life — they distract and push people onto trap-doors; practical moral: cultivate virtue to resist them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against the seductive combination of learning and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who combines charming learning (quoting classics, witty talk) with the physical signs of strutting is especially dangerous; his learning gives plausible pretext for gallantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay counsels a public warning when such men circulate (remove wives/daughters) and criticizes the false security women take from a man's erudition.
